title: Computability
summary: Which functions a Turing machine can compute: unary encoding of numbers, building bigger functions by composing machines, the µ operator for search, and the reduction to binary machines that lets 'Turing' be dropped from 'Turing computable'.

subtopics.title: Computable functions and unary representation
subtopics.summary: Numbers go on the tape in unary, with n written as n + 1 ones and multiple arguments separated by a 0. The basic computable functions are successor, predecessor, plus, times, cutoff and power.

keyFacts.definition: Throughout §2.2, ℕ denotes the natural numbers **together with zero**: ℕ = {0, 1, 2, 3, …}.
0 ↔ '1', 1 ↔ '11', 2 ↔ '111', … — the number n is written as n + 1 ones. If more than one input is used, they are **separated by a '0'**.
scsr(n) = n + 1 and pred(n) = n − 1 for n > 0 (considered in the labs); plus(m, n) = m + n (a tutorial problem); times(m, n) = m × n (Ch 7 of *Finite Automata*).
cutoff(m, n) = m − n if m ≥ n, and 0 otherwise. Written m ⊖ n.
power(m, n) = n^m — extend times the way plus was extended to give times. Note the argument order: the **first** argument is the exponent.
Any function X* → X*, for X a finite alphabet, computable by a Turing machine. This definition can be shown equivalent to the one involving natural numbers.

questions.prompt: In §2.2, what does ℕ denote?
options: The natural numbers together with zero, {0, 1, 2, 3, …}
All integers
The rationals
The positive integers {1, 2, 3, …}
questions.explanation: Zero is included — the notes open the section by fixing this. It matters throughout: cutoff returns 0, quot and sqrt search for a least q ∈ ℕ starting from 0, and the unary encoding has to have a representation for 0 at all.

questions.prompt: In the unary representation used in §2.2, how is the number **0** written on the tape?
questions.explanation: As a single '1'. The scheme is 0 ↔ '1', 1 ↔ '11', 2 ↔ '111' — so n is n + 1 ones. Encoding 0 as the empty string would be indistinguishable from a blank tape, which is why the off-by-one exists.

questions.prompt: In the unary representation of §2.2, how many 1s are written on the tape to represent the number {{n}}?

steps.text: The scheme is 0 ↔ '1', 1 ↔ '11', 2 ↔ '111', … — so each number is represented by **one more** 1 than its value.
For n = {{n}}, that is {{n}} + 1.
So {{n + 1}} ones are written.

questions.hint: Check the scheme at zero: how many 1s represent the number 0?
questions.explanation: n + 1 ones. The off-by-one is the whole content of this convention, and it is the easiest thing to get wrong when hand-tracing a numeric TM — zero is one symbol, not none.

questions.prompt: How are two arguments separated on the tape in this unary scheme?
options: By a blank symbol b
By a '0'
By a flag symbol
They are interleaved
questions.explanation: A '0'. Using b would be no good — b marks the end of the string, and the output must contain no blanks in the middle. Using 0 as the separator keeps the whole tape a string over X = {0, 1}.

questions.prompt: The function plus(m, n) is to be computed with m = {{m}} and n = {{nn}}, using the unary scheme with the two arguments separated by a single 0. How many symbols long is the input string on the tape?

steps.text: Each argument is written as (value + 1) ones: m = {{m}} takes {{m + 1}} ones, and n = {{nn}} takes {{nn + 1}} ones.
The two blocks are separated by exactly one '0', adding 1 more symbol.
Total: {{m + 1}} + 1 + {{nn + 1}} = {{m + nn + 3}} symbols.

questions.hint: Two blocks, each one longer than its value, plus a single separator between them.
questions.explanation: m + n + 3 — the two off-by-ones plus the separator. The '+3' is the tell-tale of this encoding; getting m + n + 1 means you forgot that 0 is written as '1'.

questions.prompt: Cutoff subtraction is defined by cutoff(m, n) = m − n if m {{1}} n, and {{2}} otherwise. It is written m ⊖ n.
questions.explanation: m ⊖ n = m − n when m ≥ n, and 0 otherwise. It exists because ordinary subtraction would leave ℕ — there is no −3 to write on the tape — so the result is clipped at zero.

questions.prompt: Compute the cutoff subtraction {{m}} ⊖ {{nn}}.

steps.text: cutoff(m, n) = m − n if m ≥ n, and 0 otherwise — ordinary subtraction clipped at zero, because the result must stay in ℕ.
Here m = {{m}} and n = {{nn}}. Compare them, then subtract only if m ≥ n.
Result: {{max(m - nn, 0)}}.

questions.hint: If the second number is the larger, the answer is not negative — the definition has a second clause for exactly that case.
questions.explanation: max(m − n, 0). The point of the drill is the clipping: whenever n > m the answer is 0, not a negative number, since there is no unary representation for one.

questions.prompt: The notes define diff(m, n) = |m − n| as plus(cutoff(m, n), cutoff(n, m)) = (m ⊖ n) + (n ⊖ m). Evaluate it for m = {{m}}, n = {{nn}}.

steps.text: Compute the two cutoffs separately: m ⊖ n = {{max(m - nn, 0)}} and n ⊖ m = {{max(nn - m, 0)}}.
Notice that at most one of them can be non-zero — whichever number is smaller gives 0.
Add them: {{max(m - nn, 0)}} + {{max(nn - m, 0)}} = {{abs(m - nn)}}.

questions.hint: One of the two cutoffs is always zero; the other is the gap between the numbers.
questions.explanation: |m − n|. The construction is worth understanding rather than just the answer: it computes an absolute difference using only cutoff and plus, which is how the repertoire of computable functions is enlarged without designing a new machine from scratch.

questions.prompt: The notes give max(m, n) = n + (m ⊖ n). Evaluate it for m = {{m}}, n = {{nn}}, following that formula.

steps.text: First the cutoff: m ⊖ n = {{max(m - nn, 0)}}.
Then add n: {{nn}} + {{max(m - nn, 0)}}.
= {{max(m, nn)}}. If m ≤ n the cutoff is 0 and the answer is just n; otherwise the cutoff makes up the difference to m.

questions.hint: Work the cutoff out first, then add n. Check both cases: m larger, and n larger.
questions.explanation: max(m, n), built from plus and cutoff alone. The companion formula is min(m, n) = m ⊖ (m ⊖ n), which uses cutoff twice.

questions.prompt: The notes give min(m, n) = m ⊖ (m ⊖ n). Evaluate it for m = {{m}}, n = {{nn}}, following that formula.

steps.text: Inner cutoff first: m ⊖ n = {{max(m - nn, 0)}}.
Now the outer cutoff: m ⊖ ({{max(m - nn, 0)}}) = {{m}} ⊖ {{max(m - nn, 0)}}.
= {{min(m, nn)}}. If m ≤ n the inner cutoff is 0 and the answer is m; otherwise subtracting the excess brings m down to n.

questions.hint: Two nested cutoffs — evaluate the inner one before the outer one, and clip at zero both times.
questions.explanation: min(m, n). Note it is **not** symmetric in appearance even though the result is: the formula uses m twice and n once.

questions.prompt: The notes define power(m, n) = n^m. Evaluate power({{m}}, {{nn}}).

steps.text: The definition is power(m, n) = n^m — the **first** argument is the exponent and the **second** is the base. This is the reverse of what the letters suggest.

questions.hint: Read the definition, not the letters — check carefully which argument ends up as the exponent.
questions.explanation: n^m, not m^n. Getting this backwards is the obvious trap and the reason the drill exists. It is defined by extending times the way plus was extended to give times — repeated multiplication, just as times is repeated addition.

questions.prompt: How do the notes say power is obtained?
options: By a binary Turing machine
By composing cutoff with plus
By extending times, the way plus was extended to give times
By the µ operator
questions.explanation: Repeated multiplication, mirroring how times is repeated addition. It is the same bootstrapping idea used throughout: a new function is built from machines already available rather than designed from scratch.

questions.prompt: The notes broaden Turing computability beyond functions ℕ → ℕ. To what?
options: Any relation on ℕ decidable by a TM
Any language accepted by a TM
Any function ℝ → ℝ computable by a TM
Any function X* → X*, for X a finite alphabet, computable by a Turing machine
questions.explanation: Functions from strings to strings over a finite alphabet. This subsumes the numeric case, because numbers can be represented in binary and such machines are then special cases of TMs with binary input alphabet — and the notes say the two definitions can be shown equivalent.

questions.prompt: List the computable functions ℕ → ℕ and ℕ² → ℕ that §2.2 names, and say how each is obtained.
questions.answer:
**Basic ones:**
- **scsr(n) = n + 1** and **pred(n) = n − 1** (for n > 0) — considered in the labs.
- **plus(m, n) = m + n** — a tutorial problem.
- **times(m, n) = m × n** — treated in detail in Ch 7 of *Finite Automata*.

**Further ones:**
- **cutoff(m, n) = m ⊖ n** — m − n if m ≥ n, else 0. Seen in a later lab.
- **power(m, n) = n^m** — extend times the way plus was extended to give times.

**Built by composition from those:**
- **diff(m, n) = |m − n| = (m ⊖ n) + (n ⊖ m)**
- **max(m, n) = n + (m ⊖ n)**
- **min(m, n) = m ⊖ (m ⊖ n)**

**Built by search (the µ operator):**
- **quot(m, n) = µq{(q + 1)n > m}** — m divided by n, rounded down.
- **sqrt(n) = µm{(m + 1)² > n}**

All use unary representation: n is written as n + 1 ones, with a '0' separating multiple arguments.

subtopics.title: Composing Turing machines
subtopics.summary: Make the halt state of one machine the start state of the next. It works only because a completed computation leaves the head parked.

keyFacts.definition: If M1 computes g and M2 computes h, then a TM M3 computing g(h(w)) is obtained by making the **final state of M2 into the start state of M1**, ensuring M1 and M2 otherwise have disjoint state sets.
Because we insist the head is **parked** when a computation is completed by a TM — so the second machine starts in exactly the configuration it expects, head at the left-most cell.
Compare the NFSA construction that computes the concatenation of two languages, which likewise joins the accepting states of one machine to the start states of another.

questions.prompt: M1 computes g and M2 computes h. How is a machine computing g(h(w)) built?
options: Make the final state of M2 the start state of M1, keeping the state sets otherwise disjoint
Make the final state of M1 the start state of M2
Take the union of the two transition functions
Run M1 and M2 in parallel on two tapes
questions.explanation: **M2 first** — g(h(w)) applies h first, so the inner machine runs first and hands over to M1. Getting the order backwards computes h(g(w)) instead, which is the natural slip because M1 is named first.

questions.prompt: In the composite g(h(w)), which machine reads the original input w?
options: Neither; a new machine is built from scratch
M2, the machine computing h
M1, the machine computing g
Both, on separate passes
questions.explanation: M2 computes h, and h is applied to w first. Its output h(w) is left on the tape, and M1 then runs on that, producing g(h(w)). Reading the composition inside out is the same discipline needed for σ(ρ(σ(ρ(M)))) in FSA5.

questions.prompt: Which requirement on completed computations makes the composition construction work?
options: That the tape alphabet contains a blank
That the output lies in X*
That the head is parked when a computation is completed
That δ is a partial function
questions.explanation: Parking. The second machine starts with its head at the left-most cell by definition, so the first must leave it there — otherwise M1 would begin reading in the middle of h(w). The notes say precisely this: 'This works because we insist the head is parked when a computation is completed by a TM.'

questions.prompt: Besides parking, what other requirement on a completed computation is needed for composition to be sound? Explain.
questions.answer:
That the **output v′ lies in X\*** — no blanks within the string, and no flag symbols left over.

The second machine to run expects an input that is a legitimate string over the input alphabet X, exactly as if a person had written it on a blank tape. If the first machine left behind a working symbol from Y − X, or a blank in the middle of the string, the second machine would be started on something outside its intended domain — and its behaviour there is simply not specified by whatever it was designed to compute.

So the two conditions work together: **parking** guarantees the head is where the next machine expects it, and **v′ ∈ X\*** guarantees the tape holds what the next machine expects. That is why the notes insist that just halting, or just parking, is not enough to count as completing a computation — the definition is shaped to make composition work.

questions.prompt: Why must M1 and M2 have otherwise disjoint state sets when composed?
options: So that the tape alphabets agree
So that the head stays parked
So that the composite machine is deterministic
So that a shared name does not accidentally fuse two unrelated states and let control jump between the machines
questions.explanation: State names carry no meaning, so two states with the same name would be *the same state*, creating transitions between the machines that neither design intended. Exactly the same precondition appears in the NFSA combining constructions of §1.7, and the fix is the same: rename first.

questions.prompt: The notes compare TM composition with which earlier construction?
options: The NFSA construction that computes the concatenation of two languages
The dual machine
The union of two NFSAs
The subset method
questions.explanation: Concatenation of languages. Both join the 'finished' states of one machine to the 'begin' states of another so the second picks up where the first left off — for languages with λ-edges, for TMs by identifying qf of one with q0 of the other.

questions.prompt: diff(m, n) = |m − n| is built as plus(cutoff(m, n), cutoff(n, m)). Which already-computable functions does this use?
questions.explanation: Just plus and cutoff, both already known to be computable. No new machine has to be designed for diff — this is how the repertoire is enlarged throughout §2.2.

questions.prompt: Show how max and min are obtained from cutoff and plus, and check each formula in the case m < n.
questions.answer:
**max(m, n) = n + (m ⊖ n).**
If m ≥ n, the cutoff gives m − n and adding n returns m — correct, since m is the larger.
If m < n, the cutoff clips to 0 and the answer is n + 0 = n — correct again.

**min(m, n) = m ⊖ (m ⊖ n).**
If m ≥ n, the inner cutoff gives m − n, and the outer gives m − (m − n) = n — correct.
If m < n, the inner cutoff clips to 0, and the outer gives m ⊖ 0 = m — correct, since m is the smaller.

**In the case m < n specifically**, both formulas rely on the clipping clause of cutoff: the inner subtraction would go negative, and it is the 'or 0 otherwise' branch that rescues them. Without the clip there would be no representable answer at all, since ℕ has no negative numbers to write in unary.

Both are computable because plus and cutoff are, and the composition construction glues the machines together.

questions.prompt: For partial functions, the goal is a TM that always terminates, computes the right answer when the function is defined, and does **not** terminate in the halt state when it is undefined. Why is the last condition needed?
options: Otherwise the machine would loop forever on every input
Otherwise composition would not be modelled correctly — we could get answers to compositions even when the first function is undefined
Otherwise the output would not lie in X*
Otherwise the head would not be parked
questions.explanation: The notes give exactly this reason. If a machine halted tidily on an input where its function is undefined, the next machine in a composition would happily run on whatever was left, producing a value for g(h(w)) when h(w) does not exist. Failing to reach qf is what propagates 'undefined' through the composition.

questions.prompt: The notes give f(n) = √n − 10 as an example of a partial function on ℕ. For which n is it defined?
answers: n greater than or equal to 10
questions.explanation: Only for n ≥ 10 — below that the value would not lie in ℕ. Partial functions have to be allowed because clipping is not always the right answer, and a machine must be able to signal 'no value here' by not halting.

questions.prompt: A partial function is called **Turing computable** if a TM can be built which always {{1}}, but completes a computation giving the right answer if and only if the partial function being modelled is {{2}}.
questions.explanation: Always terminates, but completes only where the function is defined. The distinction between merely terminating and *completing* — reaching qf with the head parked and a clean output — is doing real work here.

subtopics.title: The µ operator, quot and sqrt
subtopics.summary: µq{P(q)} is the least q making P true. Search upward from 0; if the truth set is non-empty this always finds it, and it yields integer division and square roots.

keyFacts.definition: µq{P(q)} means **the least q ∈ ℕ for which the predicate P(q) is true**.
If P(n) is known to have a non-empty truth set, it is easy to design a TM to compute µq{P(q)}: just let q increase from 0 until P(q) becomes true.
For m, n ∈ ℕ with n > 0, quot(m, n) = the least q ∈ ℕ such that (q + 1)n > m, written µq{(q + 1)n > m}. It is a rounded-down version of m/n.
Precision can be increased arbitrarily by multiplying by powers of 10 first and moving the decimal point back afterwards — use 10^k rather than 10 for more digits.
sqrt(n) = the least m ∈ ℕ such that (m + 1)² > n, written µm{(m + 1)² > n}. Explored in a tutorial question.

questions.prompt: What does the notation µq{P(q)} mean?
answers: the least q in N for which P(q) is true
the smallest natural number q making P(q) true
the least q such that P(q) holds
the minimum q with P(q) true
questions.explanation: The **least** q ∈ ℕ for which the predicate P(q) is true. Least, not just any — which is what makes the value well defined, by the least integer principle.

questions.prompt: How is µq{P(q)} computed by a TM, and what must be assumed?
options: Guess q and verify; assume the machine is non-deterministic
Search downwards from a known bound; assume the bound is computable
Let q increase from 0 until P(q) becomes true; assume P has a non-empty truth set
Test all q in parallel; assume P is decidable
questions.explanation: Upward search from 0, which automatically finds the *least* witness. The non-emptiness assumption is what guarantees the search terminates — with an empty truth set the machine runs forever, which is precisely the behaviour wanted for a partial function that is undefined.

questions.prompt: Why does the search start at q = 0 and increase, rather than starting anywhere else?
options: Because P(0) is always true
Because ℕ has no largest element
Because 0 is the only value a TM can write initially
Because µ demands the **least** witness, and searching upward from the smallest candidate finds that one first
questions.explanation: Ascending order is what makes the first hit the least one. Starting elsewhere might find a witness that is not minimal, giving the wrong value — and since ℕ includes 0, the smallest candidate is 0.

questions.prompt: For m, n ∈ ℕ with n {{1}} 0, quot(m, n) = µq{(q + 1)n {{2}} m}.
questions.explanation: n > 0, and the predicate is (q + 1)n > m — strictly greater. The condition n > 0 is needed because nothing divides by zero: with n = 0 the predicate (q+1)·0 > m is false for every q, and the search would never terminate.

questions.prompt: The notes work through quot(51, 24). Which sequence of tests do they perform, and what is the answer?
options: 51 ÷ 24 = 2.125, rounded to 2
questions.explanation: Test q = 0, 1, 2 in turn until the predicate first holds, at q = 2. The answer agrees with 51/24 = 2.125 rounded down, but the *method* is a search using only multiplication and comparison — the point being that a TM can do it.

questions.prompt: Compute quot({{m}}, {{nn}}) = µq{(q + 1)·{{nn}} > {{m}}} — the least q ∈ ℕ for which (q + 1)·{{nn}} exceeds {{m}}.

steps.text: The µ operator searches upward from q = 0 for the first q making (q + 1)·{{nn}} > {{m}} true.
Equivalently, find the largest multiple of {{nn}} that is still ≤ {{m}}: that multiple is q·{{nn}}, and the next one, (q + 1)·{{nn}}, overshoots.
So q is {{m}} divided by {{nn}}, rounded down: {{floor(m / nn)}}.
Check: {{floor(m / nn)}} × {{nn}} = {{floor(m / nn) * nn}} ≤ {{m}}, but {{floor(m / nn) + 1}} × {{nn}} = {{(floor(m / nn) + 1) * nn}} > {{m}}. ✓

questions.hint: Count how many whole copies of the second number fit inside the first.
questions.explanation: floor(m/n) — integer division. The verification step is the part worth internalising: the answer q must satisfy qn ≤ m **and** (q+1)n > m, so checking both sides catches an off-by-one immediately.

questions.prompt: The notes compute quot(51, 24) = 2, then quot(510, 24) = 21. What is the point of the second calculation?
options: To show quot is not well defined
To get more precision: multiplying by 10 first and moving the decimal point back gives 2.1 as a better approximation to 51/24
To show that quot(10m, n) = 10·quot(m, n)
To demonstrate that the search may fail to terminate
questions.explanation: Scaling up before dividing recovers decimal places: 21 becomes 2.1. Using 10^k rather than 10 gives as much precision as desired. Note that quot(10m, n) = 10·quot(m, n) is **false**, and these very numbers refute it: 10 × 2 = 20, not 21. That discrepancy is exactly the extra digit being recovered.

questions.prompt: Following the notes' precision trick, compute quot(10·{{m}}, {{nn}}) — the integer quotient after scaling the numerator by 10. (Dividing this by 10 afterwards gives {{m}}/{{nn}} to one decimal place.)

steps.text: First scale the numerator: 10 × {{m}} = {{10 * m}}.
Now take the integer quotient by {{nn}}, exactly as before: quot({{10 * m}}, {{nn}}) = {{floor(10 * m / nn)}}.
Moving the decimal point back one place gives {{floor(10 * m / nn) / 10}} as an approximation to {{m}}/{{nn}}.

questions.hint: Scale first, then divide — the answer is the scaled quotient, before the decimal point is moved back.
questions.explanation: floor(10m/n). Note this is generally **not** 10 × floor(m/n): the notes' own numbers show it, with quot(51,24) = 2 but quot(510,24) = 21. The extra digit is precisely the information that rounding down had discarded.

questions.prompt: Write the definition of sqrt(n) using the µ operator.
answers: the least m such that (m+1)^2 > n
questions.hint: Same shape as quot: the least value whose *successor* overshoots.
questions.explanation: sqrt(n) = µm{(m + 1)² > n} — the least m ∈ ℕ such that (m + 1)² > n. Structurally identical to quot, with squaring in place of multiplying by n.

questions.prompt: Compute sqrt({{n}}) = µm{(m + 1)² > {{n}}} — the least m ∈ ℕ whose successor squared exceeds {{n}}.

steps.text: Search upward from m = 0 for the first m with (m + 1)² > {{n}}.
Equivalently, find the largest m whose square is still ≤ {{n}}, since then (m + 1)² is the first square to overshoot.
That is the integer part of the ordinary square root: {{floor(sqrt(n))}}.
Check: {{floor(sqrt(n))}}² = {{floor(sqrt(n)) * floor(sqrt(n))}} ≤ {{n}}, but {{floor(sqrt(n)) + 1}}² = {{(floor(sqrt(n)) + 1) * (floor(sqrt(n)) + 1)}} > {{n}}. ✓

questions.hint: Which whole numbers, squared, stay at or below the target? Take the largest of them.
questions.explanation: The integer part of √n. As with quot, precision beyond the integer part is recovered by scaling — a similar method computes square roots to arbitrary precision.

questions.prompt: What happens to the upward search for µq{P(q)} if P has an **empty** truth set?
options: It returns 0
It never terminates — which is exactly the behaviour wanted when modelling a partial function that is undefined at that input
It returns the largest q tested
The machine enters qf without an output
questions.explanation: Nothing stops it, so it runs forever. Far from being a defect, this is the required behaviour for partial functions: a TM modelling one must **not** terminate in the halt state where the function is undefined, or composition would produce answers that should not exist.

questions.prompt: Explain the µ operator: what it means, how a TM computes it, what must be assumed, and how quot and sqrt use it.
questions.answer:
**Meaning.** µq{P(q)} denotes **the least q ∈ ℕ for which the predicate P(q) is true**.

**How a TM computes it.** Let q increase from 0, testing P(q) at each step, and stop at the first q that makes it true. Searching upward is what guarantees the value found is the *least* one.

**What must be assumed.** That P has a **non-empty truth set**. If it does, the search is guaranteed to stop; if it does not, the machine runs forever — which is the correct behaviour for a partial function undefined at that input, since a TM modelling one must not terminate in the halt state where there is no value.

**quot.** For n > 0, **quot(m, n) = µq{(q + 1)n > m}** — the least q whose successor, multiplied by n, overshoots m. This is m/n rounded down. The truth set is non-empty because n > 0 makes (q+1)n unbounded. Precision is recovered by scaling: compute quot(10^k·m, n) and move the decimal point back k places.

**sqrt.** **sqrt(n) = µm{(m + 1)² > n}** — the integer part of √n, by the same pattern with squaring in place of multiplying by n. A similar scaling method gives arbitrary precision.

The general lesson: **search** is a computational primitive. Anything you can test, you can search for the least instance of.

subtopics.title: Binary TMs and the Church–Turing thesis
subtopics.summary: Any TM can be re-coded to use just {0, 1} and a blank, so computability needs no alphabet. And every proposed notion of computation has turned out no stronger than Turing's.

keyFacts.definition: Suppose X is a finite alphabet and φ : X* → X* is a partial function computed by some TM with input alphabet X containing {0, 1}. Then after a suitable re-coding of the problem, φ can be computed by a TM with input alphabet just {0, 1} and tape alphabet {0, 1, b}.
A TM with X = {0, 1} and Y = {0, 1, b}. A partial function is Turing computable **if and only if** there is a binary TM that computes it.
**Any conceivable notion of computation is weaker than or equivalent to (in terms of what counts as computable) Turing computability.** This is not a theorem, but a strongly-held belief.

Many attempts to define computability have been made — for example λ-calculus — but so far all have been shown equivalent to, or weaker than, Turing computability. So it is the accepted gold standard, the adjective is dropped, and we simply say **computable**.

questions.prompt: What are the input and tape alphabets of a **binary Turing machine**?
questions.explanation: X = {0, 1}, Y = {0, 1, b} — the smallest useful tape alphabet, since Y must contain X and must contain a blank not in X.

questions.prompt: A partial function is Turing computable {{1}} there is a {{2}} Turing machine that computes it.
questions.explanation: If and only if. The forward direction is the re-coding theorem; the reverse is trivial, since a binary TM is a TM. The upshot is that the alphabet can be dropped from the definition of computability entirely.

questions.prompt: What is the significance of the re-coding theorem?
options: It shows partial functions are total
It shows binary TMs compute more functions than general TMs
It shows the alphabet is irrelevant to what is computable, so computability can be defined without reference to any particular alphabet
It shows every TM halts
questions.explanation: Nothing is gained by a richer alphabet, so 'computable' is not a notion relative to a choice of symbols. It is the same phenomenon as the flag-versus-states trade in §2.1, pushed to its limit: tape symbols can always be traded for encoding and extra states.

questions.prompt: The re-coding theorem says φ can be computed by a binary TM 'after a suitable re-coding of the problem'. What does that qualification acknowledge?
options: That the machine may fail to halt
That the theorem holds only for total functions
That the function computed may be different
That the inputs and outputs must be re-encoded as binary strings, so the binary machine computes a re-coded version of φ rather than φ on the original symbols
questions.explanation: A binary machine cannot literally read a symbol outside {0, 1}, so the data must first be encoded — each original symbol becoming a block of bits. The *content* of the computation is preserved, which is what matters for computability, but the strings on the tape are not the same ones.

questions.prompt: How do the notes state the Church–Turing Thesis?
options: Every function ℕ → ℕ is Turing computable
Any conceivable notion of computation is weaker than or equivalent to Turing computability, in terms of what counts as computable
Every Turing machine halts on every input
Turing machines and DFSAs compute the same functions
questions.explanation: 'Weaker than or equivalent to' — the thesis puts a ceiling on what any notion of computation can achieve. 'Every function ℕ → ℕ is Turing computable' is emphatically false: most functions ℕ → ℕ are not computable, since there are only countably many TMs.

questions.prompt: What is the logical status of the Church–Turing Thesis?
options: It is not a theorem, but a strongly-held belief
An axiom of the definition of a Turing machine
A conjecture known to be false
A theorem, proved via the re-coding theorem
questions.explanation: Not a theorem. It quantifies over *any conceivable* notion of computation, including ones not yet invented, and that is not a mathematical object one can quantify over in a proof. Its support is empirical: every proposal so far has turned out equivalent or weaker.

questions.prompt: Explain why the Church–Turing Thesis cannot be proved, and what evidence supports it.
questions.answer:
**Why it cannot be proved.** The thesis quantifies over **any conceivable notion of computation** — including notions nobody has proposed yet. 'Conceivable notion of computation' is an **informal** idea, not a mathematical object, so there is nothing precise to quantify over and no proof can be attempted. A proof would require first formalising the informal side, at which point one would only have proved a statement about that particular formalisation — which is exactly the kind of result the evidence already consists of.

**The evidence.** Many attempts to define computability have been made over the years, for example **λ-calculus**. So far **all have been shown to be equivalent to, or weaker than, Turing computability**. That accumulated agreement is why it is a *strongly-held belief* rather than mere speculation.

The notes add the informal test: if we can imagine writing a computer program in Java to do something, there is a TM to do it too — it may be fiendishly complex, but it exists. **Basically: if we can see an algorithmic way to do something, then there will be a TM to do it too.**

**The consequence.** Turing computability is the accepted gold standard, so the adjective is dropped and we talk simply about whether something is **computable**.
questions.hint: The obstacle is on the informal side of the claim, not the formal side.

questions.prompt: Which alternative attempt at defining computability do the notes name by way of example?
questions.explanation: λ-calculus. It is mentioned as one of many attempts, all of which have turned out equivalent to or weaker than Turing computability — the convergence that motivates the thesis.

questions.prompt: The notes offer an informal test of the thesis. What is it?
options: If a function is total then it is computable
If we can imagine writing a computer program in Java to do something, there is a TM to do it too — it may be fiendishly complex
If a DFSA can do it, a TM can do it
If a function grows slowly enough, it is computable
questions.explanation: The Java test — and more generally, if we can see an *algorithmic* way to do something then there will be a TM to do it too. It is a useful working heuristic, not an argument: 'fiendishly complex' does the work of hiding an enormous amount of construction.

questions.prompt: Why do the notes stop saying 'Turing computable' and simply say 'computable'?
options: Because computability is only defined for binary machines
Because Turing machines are the only model taught in the course
Because every proposed notion of computability has been shown equivalent to or weaker than Turing computability, so it is the generally accepted gold standard and the qualifier adds nothing
Because the re-coding theorem removes the alphabet
questions.explanation: The qualifier would only matter if some rival notion picked out a different class of functions, and none does. The re-coding theorem removes the *alphabet* from the definition; it is the Church–Turing thesis that removes the *model*.

questions.prompt: §2.2 gives a numeric notion of computability (functions ℕ → ℕ, in unary) and a string notion (functions X* → X*). What is their relationship?
options: The numeric notion applies only to total functions
They are unrelated
The string notion is strictly more general and computes more functions
It can be shown that the two definitions of computability are equivalent
questions.explanation: Equivalent — the notes say so directly. Numbers can be represented in binary, so numeric machines are special cases of TMs with binary input alphabet; and conversely strings can be coded as numbers. It is the same reduction-by-encoding idea as the re-coding theorem.

questions.prompt: State the re-coding theorem and the Church–Turing Thesis, and say what each one lets you stop worrying about.
questions.answer:
**Re-coding theorem.** Suppose X is a finite alphabet and φ : X* → X* is a partial function computed by some TM with input alphabet X containing {0, 1}. Then **after a suitable re-coding of the problem, φ can be computed by a TM with input alphabet just {0, 1} and tape alphabet {0, 1, b}** — a **binary Turing machine**. Hence a partial function is Turing computable **if and only if** some binary TM computes it.

*What it lets you stop worrying about:* **the alphabet**. No richer set of symbols buys any extra computing power, so computability is not relative to a choice of symbols. (This is the flag-versus-states trade of §2.1 taken to its limit.)

**Church–Turing Thesis.** **Any conceivable notion of computation is weaker than or equivalent to — in terms of what counts as computable — Turing computability.**

It is **not a theorem, but a strongly-held belief**, because it quantifies over informal notions of computation and so has nothing precise to be proved about. The evidence is that many attempts, λ-calculus among them, have all turned out equivalent or weaker.

*What it lets you stop worrying about:* **the model**. Turing computability is the gold standard, so the adjective is dropped and we say simply **computable**.
